Reasoning

1. The singlet at 2.1 ppm integrating for 3 H is typical of the acetyl methyl of an acetate ester (–O–COCH₃).

2. Besides that singlet the spectrum shows only:
   • two one-proton vinylic signals (7.0 ppm and 5.5 ppm)  
   • one vinylic-methyl doublet (1.6 ppm, 3 H, d, J ≈ 7 Hz).

   There is no signal for a methylene group (2 H).  
   Therefore the side chain contains only three carbons (CH₃–CH=CH–), not four; the compound is a propenyl acetate, not a butenyl acetate.

3. The two vinylic protons are coupled to each other with J = 16 Hz (the 7.0 ppm doublet).  
   A vicinal coupling constant of about 16 Hz is characteristic of a trans (E) alkene; cis (Z) alkenes show J ≈ 10 Hz.

4. The vinylic proton at 5.5 ppm is split into a doublet of quartets because it is
   • trans-coupled (J ≈ 16 Hz) to the other vinyl proton, and  
   • coupled (J ≈ 7 Hz) to the adjacent methyl group (1.6 ppm, d).

Thus the unknown is the trans (E) isomer of propenyl acetate.

Answer: B
